doc.title: Steve Wilson interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, October 25, 2002

chapter: The music industry and the press
title: Gary Peacock, Albert Ayler and critics
summary: The Ayler story that his music was about nothing, and composers complaining about critics.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: Critics, polls and the jazz press

blocks.x: I love that statement you just made in passing, and that was “I wasn’t thinking of anything when I wrote that.” I mean can you talk about that? Because I think it’s a very interesting thing and like you said I think sometimes we have to put a meaning on everything.

Yeah. I remember having a conversation about three years ago with Gary Peacock. We were both doing the Montreal Festival. And I had never met him before and I had a really fascinating conversation with him. I was very honored that he was talking to me. But he told me about an instance when he was working with I think Albert Ayler or somebody like that. And of course at that time they were being pegged the angry black musicians, because they’re playing avante garde or so-called avante garde. And Albert had read some review and whoever the writer was was talking about oh we can hear the anger and about being oppressed and about Vietnam and about this and about that. And Albert said, “Man, it ain’t about nothing. It ain’t about nothing.” You know? So that stuck with me. Because a lot of times these writers, when you read these reviews, they will write something and it says that they’re trying to tell the audience what we’re trying to do. It’s like well at least give us the courtesy of coming to us to let us explain what agenda we have, if any. Rather than taking this upon themselves to interpret our music for the benefit of the audience. No. And there’s another interesting book, I think called Composers on Music which I had some years ago and lost it somewhere along the way. But it had composers from I think like Bach on through to Aaron Copland, and where they read reviews of their works and they were dealing with the same issues, where the critics were talking about how invalid their particular work was, or finding anything wrong with it that they could just to advance their own agenda, I’m talking about the writer. And it had the musicians writing to either like relatives or to each other in some instances, saying this critic is totally out of his mind, it had nothing to do with what I was working towards in this piece of music. So it’s an age-old issue. It’s nothing new.
